papers.title: InstAgent: A Recursively Self-Improving Agent Operating System for Heterogeneous Robot Collaboration
papers.summary: Heterogeneous robot teams enable complex, long-horizon tasks by combining complementary sensing, mobility, and manipulation capabilities across multiple embodiments. Yet existing systems struggle to retain execution-time corrections as reusable experience, maintain task-relevant context memory across space and time for reliable handoffs, and explicitly represent the inter-robot dependencies required for structured collaboration. In order to address these challenges, we present InstAgent, a recursively self-improving (RSI) Agent Operating System for heterogeneous robot collaboration. InstAgent organizes team behaviors as agentic behavior trees (BTs) that explicitly model capability assignment, inter-robot dependencies and handoff checks. The RSI mechanism updates these collaboration programs from execution feedback and preserves successful revisions for reuse in future tasks, while shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory provides context for planning and handoff validation. Experiments on 20 real-world multi-robot tasks with three high-level models show consistent gains in task success, first-attempt completion, and execution efficiency.

papers.title: Cloud‐Native and Distributed Systems for Efficient and Scalable Large Language Models—A Research Agenda
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Objective Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming artificial intelligence applications, but their unprecedented computational, memory, communication, and data‐management demands pose significant challenges to existing computing infrastructures. Traditional cloud and distributed systems were not designed for the scale, dynamic execution patterns, heterogeneous hardware requirements, and service‐level demands of modern LLM workloads. This paper aims to examine how cloud‐native and distributed systems can evolve to support efficient, scalable, reliable, and sustainable LLM training and inference. Methods We conduct a structured analysis of representative research advances and practical developments in distributed LLM training, inference serving, cloud‐native orchestration, resource management, heterogeneous computing, and edge‐cloud intelligence. We organize the analysis around major system challenges, including computation, distributed execution and system software, resource management and serving, security and privacy, data management, and standardization. We further examine representative resource‐management strategies and emerging paradigms, including serverless inference, federated and decentralized learning, trustworthy distributed AI, and heterogeneous computing with emerging accelerators. papers.title: The shift toward open and reproducible AI research
papers.summary: Abstract The reproducibility crisis has directed the AI research community toward improving documentation practices. Several studies have identified methodological issues, and in response, the most impactful venues in the field have introduced reproducibility checklists. We seek to understand whether documentation practices have changed over time by assessing all published papers at five leading AI conferences over the past decade. Seven reproducibility variables were identified, quality-assured and used to analyse 56,800 publications. Our analysis reveals that in the period 2014 to 2024, documentation practices have improved; papers sharing both code and data increased nearly sixfold, from 11% to 64%. Building on empirical reproducibility rates from a prior study, we estimate – inferred from documentation practices, not direct testing – that reproducibility increased from 28% in 2014 to 64% in 2024. Improvements in documentation practices predate the introduction of reproducibility checklists, suggesting these changes reflect a broader movement toward open science rather than a direct response to formal requirements.

papers.title: A PRIVACY PRESERVING PERSONAL AI ASSISTANT AND THE COST OF CLOUD MODEL INFERENCE: ARCHITECTURE, CAPABILITY TRADEOFFS, AND EVALUATION PROTOCOL
papers.summary: Personal AI assistants need reliable research and controlled access to private data. This report specifies a local-first Windows architecture and examines the capability, privacy, and operating-cost tradeoff between local Llama 3.2 3B through Ollama and self-hosted Kimi K2.5 on rented NVIDIA GPUs. We analyzed a supplied project design summary, mapped trust boundaries and failure modes, and calculated illustrative costs from a documented eight-H200 deployment and published rental rates. The design separates public research from authenticated browser sessions, enforces permissions outside the model, and requires evidence-supported answers. At an illustrative $4.59 per GPU-hour, eight H200s cost $36.72 per running hour, $4,406.40 for four hours daily over 30 days, or $26,438.40 for continuous 30-day operation, before storage and operations. An assumed 100 W incremental local draw for four hours daily at $0.15/kWh costs $1.80 monthly on an existing PC. These are scenarios, not measured deployments. Kimi K2.5 offers multimodal and agentic capabilities that a text-only 3B baseline should not be assumed to match; no matched end-to-end test was performed. Stronger cloud inference can impose substantial dedicated GPU rental cost and transfers prompts to a cloud operator. Local inference preserves a narrower data boundary at far lower incremental cash cost but requires direct task-qualit

papers.title: DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses
papers.summary: Scientific discovery requires developing worthwhile hypotheses into practical investigations, yet learning from this evolving research process remains challenging. We introduce an operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses: evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties, coupled with feasible investigations, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations. Our DiscoveryRSI framework develops hypothesis trees through multi-agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and recursively learns through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization attributes scientific assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay identifies productive strategies and recurring failures to refine research workflows; and rediscovery applies accepted improvements to new investigations, generating further experience for subsequent learning. We also introduce DFM-Bench, which provides comprehensive assessment of hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress at the levels of hypotheses, revisions, development paths and research runs. Across four life-science domains, automated evaluation shows that hypothesis quality rises from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self-improvement, with the large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability. We further validate hypothesis

papers.title: MLOps-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Production ML Engineering in Real Repositories
papers.summary: AI agents are increasingly expected to modify and maintain machine-learning systems in production, yet existing benchmarks primarily evaluate either competition-style ML experimentation or generic repository issue resolution. We introduce MLOps-Bench, a repository-grounded benchmark for production ML engineering. Unlike prior ML-agent benchmarks, MLOps-Bench evaluates executable lifecycle changes inside real ML repositories, spanning data pipelines, feature engineering, model training, model serving, monitoring, CI/CD and governance, and end-to-end integration. Each task is grounded in repository evidence and includes a natural-language requirement, oracle patch, plausible buggy baseline, fail-to-pass tests, pass-to-pass tests, and provenance metadata. The benchmark contains 212 validated tasks from 31 public ML repositories, with 636 fail-to-pass tests and 856 pass-to-pass tests. We evaluate six agents and find that the best system solves 31.2% of tasks while passing 68.7% of tests, showing that current agents often make partial progress but still fail production-relevant behavioral requirements. MLOps-Bench shifts agent evaluation beyond model building and issue fixing toward repository-native MLOps work where correctness depends on lifecycle reasoning, behavioral robustness, and preservation of existing system behavior.

papers.title: Design and Evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence–Based Model for Predicting Twelfth-Grade Students’ Mathematics Performance Based on Individual, Educational, and Learning Technology Factors
papers.summary: Purpose: This study aimed to design and evaluate an artificial intelligence–based model for predicting the mathematics performance of twelfth-grade experimental sciences students based on individual, educational, and learning technology factors. Methods and Materials: This applied, quantitative, cross-sectional, and predictive study was conducted among twelfth-grade experimental sciences students in Isfahan, Iran. A total of 187 questionnaires were distributed, and after removing incomplete, inconsistent, and invalid records, data from 84 students were retained for analysis. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire assessing individual factors, educational conditions, and learning technology variables, together with students’ recorded mathematics scores. The dataset was divided into training and testing subsets, and repeated five-fold cross-validation was used for internal model development. Multiple linear regression, ridge regression, lasso regression, elastic net regression, decision tree regression, random forest regression, gradient boosting regression, and support vector regression were compared. Model performance was evaluated using mean absolute error, root mean squared error, and the coefficient of determination. Findings: Previous mathematics achievement had the strongest positive correlation with current mathematics performance, followed by mathematics se

papers.title: Development of an LLM-Based System for Automatic Code Generation from HEP Publications
papers.summary: Ensuring the reproducibility of physics results is one of the crucial challenges in high-energy physics (HEP). In this study, we develop a proof-of-concept system that uses large language models (LLMs) to extract analysis procedures from HEP publications and generate executable analysis code for reproducing published results. Our method consists of two stages. In the first stage, open-weight LLMs extract event selection criteria, object definitions, and other relevant analysis information from a target paper and, when necessary, from its referenced publications, and then produce a structured selection list. In the second stage, the structured selection list is used to generate analysis code, which is then executed and validated iteratively. As a benchmark, we use the ATLAS $H \rightarrow ZZ^{*} \rightarrow 4\ell$ analysis based on proton-proton collision data recorded in 2015 and 2016 and released as ATLAS Open Data. This benchmark allows direct comparison between the generated results and the published analysis, as well as comparison with a manually developed baseline implementation. We separately evaluate selection extraction and code generation in order to clarify the current capabilities and limitations of open-weight LLMs for HEP analysis reproduction. Our initial results show that recent open-weight models can recover many documented selection criteria from papers and ref

papers.title: From Prompting to Engineering: A Research Agenda for Prompt Engineering in Software Engineering
papers.summary: Prompt engineering is increasingly used across Software Engineering (SE) activities, including requirements analysis, coding, testing, documentation, repository analysis, and planning. Yet prompts and related instruction artifacts are often created and evolved through task-specific and informal practices, with limited support for their systematic evaluation, management, traceability, and governance. To examine how SE can contribute to the maturation of these practices, we organized a structured community discussion at the First International Workshop on Empirical Prompt Engineering for Software Engineering (PROMPTSE), co-located with EASE 2026. Participants discussed current prompting practices, challenges to their adoption and evaluation, and future directions for integrating prompt engineering into software development. We synthesized these discussions into five areas: prompt artifacts and standardization; evaluation and benchmarking; lifecycle integration; human–AI collaboration and skills; and governance, privacy, and technical debt. Based on these areas, we outline a research agenda to move prompt engineering from predominantly ad hoc interactions toward more systematic, maintainable, evaluable, traceable, and governable SE practices.

papers.title: From Approval to Abuse: Privilege Escalation Attacks on Harness-Protected Coding Agents
papers.summary: Coding agents use execution harnesses to constrain the consequences of prompt injection by enforcing permission boundaries. These systems deterministically intercept any out-of-sandbox action and prompt the user for approval. To reduce approval fatigue, users can approve allow-rules proposed by the agent, after which any future action matching the rule is allowed without a prompt. In this work, we show that this mechanism introduces a new risk: untrusted context can influence the permissions presented for approval, with consequences extending beyond the immediate task. We investigate privilege escalation targeting this permission-update process. Specifically, adversarial context planted in a repository can reliably steer an agent performing a routine task into requesting a plausibly justified, yet dangerously broad allow-rule. If the user approves the request, the saved rule can effectively blind the harness, enabling adversaries to execute malicious actions that would otherwise require approval, without triggering human oversight. Across production platforms, including Claude Code and Codex CLI, we demonstrate that agents successfully elicit the target allow-rules in 58% of experimental instances. Once acquired, these rules exhibit a massive semantic blast radius, covering 56.9% of category-specific capability test cases. To further quantify the downstream risk, we show that c

papers.title: Beyond Reward Scoring: Online Multi-Agent Preference Learning for Multimodal Response Generation
papers.summary: Multimodal preference alignment often follows a score-based RLHF pipeline: a reward model is first trained to learn human preferences, then used to score on-policy responses and optimize the response model's generation. This turns preference supervision into a scalar signal for generation: a model may learn to produce answers with higher preference scores, but is rarely trained explicitly to learn the reasons underlying human preferences. We therefore ask whether making preference understanding an internal capability of the response model can improve its generation. To investigate this question, we propose \textbf{PrefMind}, an online dual-agent reinforcement learning framework with two trainable agents: a response Generator and a preference Critic. Given a pair of candidate responses, the agents analyze and discuss which response better aligns with human preference. Human labels supervise their judgments and corrections. For pairs on which both the Generator and revised Critic correctly identify the human-preferred response, the Generator produces an improved answer, and the Critic compares it against the original preferred response to provide a generation reward. Both agents are jointly updated from interactions sampled with their current policies. Through this process, \textbf{PrefMind} trains the Generator to understand human preferences via explicit judgment and correction

papers.title: CarBench: A comprehensive benchmark for neural surrogates on high-fidelity 3D car aerodynamics
papers.summary: Abstract Benchmarking has been the cornerstone of progress in computer vision, natural language processing, and the broader deep learning domain, driving algorithmic innovation through standardized datasets and reproducible evaluation protocols. The growing availability of large-scale Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) datasets has opened new opportunities for applying machine learning to aerodynamic and engineering design. Yet, despite this progress, large-scale standardized benchmarks remain limited for high-resolution three-dimensional automotive aerodynamics, making it difficult to evaluate and compare models systematically. In this work, we introduce CarBench, a large-scale standardized benchmark dedicated to high-resolution 3D automotive aerodynamics, and perform a large-scale evaluation of state-of-the-art models on DrivAerNet++, the largest public dataset for automotive aerodynamics, containing over 8,000 high-fidelity car simulations. We assess eleven representative model configurations spanning multiple modeling paradigms: classical neural operator methods (e.g., Fourier Neural Operator), geometric deep learning approaches (PointNet, RegDGCNN, PointMAE, PointTransformer), transformer-based neural solvers (Transolver, Transolver++, AB-UPT), and implicit field networks leveraging triplane representations (TripNet). papers.title: AppFlow: Memory Scheduling for Cold Launch of Large Apps on Mobile and Vehicle Systems
papers.summary: GB-scale large apps like on-device LLMs and rich media editors are becoming the next-generation trend, but their heavy memory and I/O demands, especially during multitasking, cause devices to reclaim or kill processes, turning warm apps into cold launches. The challenge lies not in storing them, but in fast, accurate launching. For users, 1s is the usability cliff, yet our measurements show 86.6\% of GB-scale cold launches exceed it. Also, Android Vitals flags only $\geq$ 5s as slow, exposing a large satisfaction gap. Existing optimizations are designed in isolation and conflict. For example, preloading reduces I/O stalls but consumes scarce memory and is undone by reclamation, while reclamation and killing free memory but sacrifice background survivability, leading to repeated cold relaunches. Our key insight is that, although multitasking makes runtime behavior complex, each app's file access pattern remains predictable. The challenge lies in exploiting this predictability, i.e., preloading without exhausting memory, reclaiming without undoing gains, and killing selectively to preserve background survivability. We introduce AppFlow, a prediction-based system-wide scheduler that integrates a Selective File Preloader, an Adaptive Memory Reclaimer, and a Context-Aware Process Killer. Implemented across the Android framework and Linux kernel without app changes, AppFlow cuts GB-s

Recent Developments in Intrusion Detection for the Internet of Underwater Things: A Systematic Review
papers.summary: The Internet of Underwater Things (IoUT) has significantly improved underwater communication. However, due to the unique and challenging characteristics of underwater acoustic channels, such as long multipaths, high propagation delay and Doppler variation, and severe energy and bandwidth limitation, IoUT networks are highly vulnerable to security threats. These conditions make conventional Internet of Things (IoT) intrusion detection systems (IDS) less effective. Improving the security of IoUT networks requires specialised intrusion detection approaches tailored to address these challenges. This paper reviews intrusion detection in IoUT. It describes the architecture of IoUT networks, and demonstrates how the channel dynamics affect the capabilities of an IDS. It also categorises threats across the physical, data link, network, transport, and application layers, together with cross-layer attacks, insider threats, and advanced persistent threats. Furthermore, the review compares anomaly-based, trust-based, and hybrid detection frameworks, with emphasis on machine learning, federated learning, blockchain-assisted security, and density-based clustering. The results are compared based on evaluation metrics, latency, energy efficiency, and computational complexity. Finally, the paper outlines open challenges and future research directions, focusing on cross-layer detection, communic

papers.title: Clinically guided subgroup-aware framework for dental implant risk stratification using expert-informed feature selection and cross-group knowledge transfer
papers.summary: Dental implant outcome prediction is challenging due to the interplay of systemic health variables, oral conditions, and anatomical parameters. Existing machine learning approaches often treat patient populations as homogeneous and optimize a single global feature subset. This approach limits sensitivity to subgroup-specific risk patterns, reduces interpretability, and weakens the detection of high-risk failure cases. This study proposes TBLPSO, a team-based learning particle swarm optimization framework that integrates clinically guided subgrouping, expert-informed initialization, reliability-aware weighting of expert input, and cross-group feature collaboration. Patients are stratified into four clinically meaningful subgroups: Low Risk, Local Risk, Systemic Risk, and Complex Case, using a real-world European dental implant dataset comprising a total of 55 clinical features. The dataset was chronologically divided into training and testing sets, and five-fold temporal cross-validation was applied to the training set. Each subgroup is optimized independently while selectively sharing predictive features across groups. This enables the model to capture both subgroup-specific and generalizable risk factors. Extensive comparisons with PSO variants, wrapper-based methods, evolutionary algorithms, and standard classifiers demonstrate that TBLPSO consistently outperforms these metho

Digital-Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance and Fault-Tolerant Control for Electrified Agricultural Machinery: A Multiphysics and Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for PMSM In-Wheel Drives
papers.summary: Electrified agricultural machinery increasingly relies on permanent-magnet synchronous motor drives that must remain dependable under variable traction, terrain-induced vibration, thermal cycling, contamination, and intermittent duty. Existing work offers mature methods for motor fault diagnosis, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and distributed-drive fault-tolerant control, but their health information is often not shared across diagnosis, maintenance, and control. This article develops a multiphysics digital-twin framework in which electrical, thermal, mechanical, and vibrational evidence maintains a probabilistic health belief that constrains both supervisory maintenance decisions and torque redistribution. The framework formalizes observability, uncertainty-aware health factors, deterministic safety shielding, multi-rate fallback logic, and agriculture-specific traction constraints. Reproducible low-fidelity numerical studies provide preliminary support for context-conditioned residual diagnosis and the revised thermal-continuity trade-off underlying health-aware derating, including robustness and sensitivity analyses. They do not validate sim-to-real transfer or the reinforcement-learning policy itself; those hypotheses remain open for dynamometer and hardware-in-the-loop testing. The results are therefore interpreted as mechanism-level evidence rather than field-perf

papers.title: Exploring or Exploiting Generative AI? A Dual-Path, Dual-Horizon Theory of Employee Incremental and Radical Creativity
papers.summary: Recent research has established that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is not a unitary workplace resource: exploratory and exploitative use orientations are associated with different forms of employee creativity, and their value depends on employees' capacity to integrate generated knowledge. This article therefore does not present the basic dual path as a new discovery. Instead, it develops a theoretical integration and dynamic extension that asks why the established paths operate differently, when employees should switch between them, and how short-run augmentation can evolve into either capability accumulation or capability substitution. We distinguish expansive and consolidative modes of knowledge integration, theorize phase-congruent switching rather than static ``high-high'' ambidexterity, and position metacognition as a control mechanism that governs both immediate knowledge conversion and longer-run cognitive development. We further specify cultural tightness and psychological safety as directional boundary conditions and distinguish individual creative gains from collective idea-space diversity. The framework converts emerging empirical regularities into falsifiable propositions about task phase, context, and time, providing a research agenda for sustainable human--AI creativity.

papers.title: Metaverse and NFT-Based Digital Ecosystems: Sustainability, Governance, and Energy Trade-Offs
papers.summary: Metaverse platforms and non-fungible token (NFT) markets are often framed as immaterial, frictionless layers of the digital economy. However, their expansion depends on energy-intensive infrastructures, complex governance arrangements, and regulatory choices that can amplify or mitigate environmental externalities. This article examines sustainability, governance, and energy trade-offs in metaverse and NFT-based ecosystems. The research treats China as a policy and regulatory laboratory. This is to explore the ideas of how "digital collectibles" and platform-based experiments have evolved under tighter constraints on cryptocurrency circulation. Building on a socio-technical perspective, the paper connects three levels of analysis. It maps the material footprint of immersive experiences and tokenized assets, focusing on consensus mechanisms, cloud and data center dependencies, and the risk of rebound effects. The exploration of governance addresses technical standards and platform accountability. In the meantime, it discusses the tensions between openness, interoperability, and enforceable rules. A comparison of regulatory pathways addresses their implications for sustainability metrics, user rights, and market design. The contribution of this research lies in the framework for evaluating whether metaverse and NFT ecosystems can credibly align with sustainability goals without r

papers.title: The new constructionism. Papert after Peirce: indexicality, navigational thinking, and learning in the age of generative AI
papers.summary: The arrival of generative AI in every classroom has produced a crisis that is at once technological, epistemological, and pedagogical. We argue that the appropriate response is neither prohibition nor naive adoption, but a principled reconstruction of constructionism for a computational environment that is generative, context-sensitive, and dialogically accessible. Drawing on Peircean semiotics, Papertian constructionism, Polanyi's epistemology, and contemporary neural-network research, we develop a programmatic framework we call the New Constructionism. We make four connected contributions. First, we argue that generative AI introduces an indexical mode of computation: its relation to the empirical world may be direct, mediated, or incomplete, but in a situated human–AI configuration meaning is operationally conditioned by conversational history, artifacts, tools, observations, and action. Second, we introduce a three-dimensional analytical space — semiotic, psycho-epistemological, and pedagogical — in which learning paradigms can be located and compared. Third, we reinterpret the history of programming education as a movement from a predominantly symbolic environment toward a hybrid ecology in which symbolic execution, distributional generation, and situated reference coexist. This hybridity qualifies but does not cancel the indexical turn at the level of interaction and educ

papers.title: The double-edged sword effect of AI technological disruption awareness on design innovation competence: the mediating role of regulatory focus and the moderating role of AI critical thinking
papers.summary: Introduction: While the rapid advancement of AI technology is empowering design practice, it is also having a significant impact on the development of design innovation education. In the context of design education, how students' perceived “AI technological disruption awareness (AITDA)” influences their design innovation competence has become a critical issue. Existing research has largely focused on the negative effects of technological disruption, overlooking the complex psychological mechanisms that may be triggered within design learning environments. Methods Drawing on regulatory focus theory (RFT), this study examines how students' AI technological disruption awareness (AITDA) is associated with their design innovation competence (DIC) through two parallel motivational pathways, promotion focus (ProF) and prevention focus (PreF), and whether AI critical thinking (AICT) moderates these pathways. A questionnaire survey was administered to 568 design students from Chinese universities, and the moderated dual-path model was tested with confirmatory factor analysis, hierarchical regression, and bootstrap-based mediation and moderated-mediation analyses. Results The results show that AITDA was significantly positively associated with DIC, both directly and through the positive pathway of ProF, whereas it was simultaneously significantly negatively associated with DIC through th

papers.title: Using AI to Build Student Feedback Literacy and Leverage Assessment as a Learning Tool
papers.summary: This conceptual article explores practical ways in which college and university instructors can leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to support assessment as learning and develop students’ feedback literacy. Traditional assessment practices often focus on assessment for learning (informing instruction) or of learning (measuring outcomes), while assessment as learning—when students actively monitor and reflect on their own learning—receives less attention. AI can help instructors leverage assessment as a learning tool by generating work samples for student analysis and providing timely, actionable feedback that students can use to revise their work. When combined with instructor modeling, peer dialogue, and scaffolds such as guiding questions or graphic organizers, AI-supported feedback promotes metacognition, self-directed learning, and critical evaluation skills. The article provides practical guidance, including prompts and strategies for using AI to enhance student engagement with feedback, helping instructors create more efficient, effective, and student-centered practices that utilize assessments as learning tools.

papers.title: Video and digital games: Historical controversies, benefits, and risks for children and adolescents
papers.summary: Video and digital games have been the focus of sustained public and scientific debate since their commercial emergence in the late 1970s, particularly regarding their effects on children and adolescents. Early public and scientific discourse frequently portrayed gaming as a source of physical injury, addiction, aggression, social isolation, academic problems, and moral decline. However, subsequent empirical research has produced a substantially more differentiated picture of both the benefits and risks of gaming. This review examines the historical foundations of controversies surrounding video and digital games and synthesizes contemporary evidence concerning their cognitive, emotional, social, therapeutic, and physical effects. . Research indicates that moderate, purposeful gaming may improve visuospatial abilities, attentional control, problem-solving, mood regulation, social connection, and selected educational outcomes. Gaming-based interventions have also demonstrated therapeutic potential, particularly for depressive symptoms and attention-related difficulties among young people. At the same time, important risks remain, especially when gaming becomes excessive, compulsive, or disruptive to everyday functioning. These include repetitive-strain injuries, sleep disruption, problematic gaming, and adverse mental-health and academic outcomes. Evidence concerning violent game

papers.title: The k-Flip Ising game
papers.summary: The game-theoretic view on the classical Ising model – the noisy binary choice Ising game, - is a well-known conceptual framework that, on the one hand, highlights similar patterns between social agent-based systems, artificial systems of binary units such as neural networks and ensembles of interacting physical spins and, on the other hand, helps to stress important differences between them. This study considers one of the aspects that is, in principle, common to all these fields, but seems to be more relevant to gametheoretic setting than, e.g., to kinetics of spin systems - the possibility of simultaneous decision making of several agents that is typical for game theoretic interaction. In this work we analyse a partially parallel discrete time dynamics of an Ising-type system of N interacting binary units on a complete graph in which at each time step k arbitrarily chosen units can change their states is analysed. The particular problem under study is a k - dependence of the decay of a metastable configuration into a stable one. The analysis is based on an explicit analytical calculation, for arbitrary noise, of the transition matrix characterising, for a given N, the k - flip evolution as well as the first two moments of the distribution of the fraction of players choosing one of the two available strategies. papers.title: Drift‐Corrected Monocular VIO and Perception‐Aware Planning for Autonomous Drone Racing
papers.summary: ABSTRACT The Abu Dhabi Autonomous Racing League (A2RL) x Drone Champions League (DCL) competition requires teams to perform high‐speed autonomous drone racing using only a single camera and a low‐quality inertial measurement unit—a minimal sensor set that mirrors expert human drone racing pilots. This sensor limitation makes the system susceptible to drift from Visual‐Inertial Odometry (VIO), particularly during long and fast flights with aggressive maneuvers. This paper presents the system developed for the championship. Our approach corrects VIO drift by fusing its output with global position measurements derived from a YOLO‐based gate detector using a Kalman filter, reducing the translational error by 46% relative to the VIO only. A perception‐aware planner generates trajectories that balance speed with the need to keep gates visible for the perception system, improving gate visibility by 16%. The system demonstrated high performance, securing podium finishes across multiple categories: third place in the AI Grand Challenge with a top speed of 43.2 km/h, second place in the AI Drag Race with over 59 km/h, and second place in the AI Multi‐Drone Race. We detail the complete architecture and present a performance analysis based on experimental data from the competition, contributing our insights into building a successful system for monocular vision‐based autonomous drone fligh

papers.title: Level 2.5 large deviations and uncertainty relations for self-interacting jump processes: Tilting constructions and the emergence of time-scale separation
papers.summary: Self-interacting jump processes (SIJPs) describe systems with non-Markovian stochastic dynamics in which transition rates depend on empirical observables of the process, which gives rise to long-range memory and feedback. We derive the ``level-2.5'' large deviation (LD) principle governing the joint fluctuations of empirical occupation measure and the flux matrix for a broad class of SIJPs with general functional dependence on an empirical observable. The derivation is based on an exponential tilting construction and reveals a separation between a faster timescale of the microscopic dynamics and a slower timescale of the memory-driven evolution of transition rates, which is expressed through an exponentially discounted LD rate functional. Using this variational framework, we derive kinetic and thermodynamic uncertainty relations that extend classical Markovian bounds to non-Markovian systems, and illustrate their performance with simple examples.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal quantum advantages for rare-event sampling
papers.summary: In a world fraught with uncertainty, it behooves us to consider the most disastrous possible outcomes, in order that we can best mitigate against them. Often these are extreme risk events -- of high consequence, but low probability. Yet, the rarity of such events limits our ability to study them; there is a paucity of past occurrences to draw upon, and sampling such rare events from models is typically costly in time. Here, we introduce an approach for rare-event sampling based on quantum stochastic models. This integrates the memory advantages of quantum stochastic modelling -- and its associated efficient means of preparing quantum sample states -- with the `speed-ups' of quantum amplitude amplification, to yield simultaneous reductions in spatial and temporal computational complexity compared to classical Monte Carlo-based approaches.

papers.title: Empirical Software Engineering in Practice: Insights from Google
papers.summary: While it is fairly well known how empirical software engineering (ESE) is used in the academic world, we have limited knowledge of how ESE is practiced in industry. As part of our regular column on empirical software engineering (ACM SIGSOFT SENESE), we want to dedicate a series of articles to interviewing ESE practitioners from various companies. Among other things, we want to understand how ESE processes are implemented in industry, e.g., different research methods, how practitioners decide on what to study, how research results are used within companies and beyond, and if they face recurrent impediments to using ESE methods in industrial contexts. In the first edition of ESE in Practice, we are joined by Ciera Jaspan and Collin Green from the Developer Intelligence team at Google. This article is a faithful account of our conversation from August 13, 2026, which we edited for our column.
